title: What is known about 1RB1RA_1RC0RE_0RD1LE_0LE---_1LF0LC_0RA1LC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RA_1RC0RE_0RD1LE_0LE---_1LF0LC_0RA1LC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The tape is made of the six-cell word 010111 in its rotations. The crossing moves of A and B over it are proved in Lean. On the left, the word is cut by single 1s into runs whose lengths are 2k − 1 in 99.6% of samples, so two equal runs and the 1 between them make the next size, as in a binary carry. How the runs are created and merged is not proved, and the halting transition (D reading a 1) is not ruled out.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 45,385 cells have been visited and 30,990 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.476). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.31).

claims.title: Crossing the periodic word
claims.text: A crosses (010111)^n, (101011)^n, (110101)^n and (111010)^n to the right, leaving (101111)^n, (110111)^n, (111011)^n and (111101)^n. B crosses (101110)^n, leaving (011111)^n. All for every n.

claims.title: Run lengths 2<sup>k</sup> − 1
claims.text: In the last 200 samples before step 2·109 (state F at the left end, the tape read in the words s = 111010 etc.), 259,121 of the 260,035 runs 1 s^n 1 have n = 2k − 1.

claims.title: Crossing the periodic word
claims.text: A crosses (010111)^n, (101011)^n, (110101)^n and (111010)^n to the right, leaving (101111)^n, (110111)^n, (111011)^n and (111101)^n. B crosses (101110)^n, leaving (011111)^n. All for every n.

claims.title: Run lengths 2<sup>k</sup> − 1
claims.text: In the last 200 samples before step 2·109 (state F at the left end, the tape read in the words s = 111010 etc.), 259,121 of the 260,035 runs 1 s^n 1 have n = 2k − 1.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The machine halts only when D reads a 1. D is entered from C on a 0 (writing 0, moving right), at the boundary of a run. A halt would need a run boundary of an unusual shape. No invariant ruling that out has been found. CTL (windows of 2 to 5 cells) and NGramCPS (widths 2 to 8, history, LRU) fail.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has run for 10<sup>9</sup> steps without stopping. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and lists what is known, each result marked by what it rests on.

sections.heading: One word, many runs
html:
Read in six-cell words (q = 101011, r = 110101, s = 111010), the tape at a moment when F is at the left end looks like this (step 37,591,608, abridged):

F>0 q^462 1 0 s^13 1 s^126 1 s^127 1 s^127 1 s^127 1 s^127 1 s^95 1 s^17 1^3 0
    s^6 1 s^15 1 s^15 1 s^15 1 s^5 1 s^3 1 s^3 1 s^3 1 s^3 1 s 1^3 0 1 s 1 s ... 1^3 0
A sweep to the right crosses each run in one go. A turns 111010 into 111101 and the other rotations likewise (proved in Lean for every run length). The next sweep restores them.

sections.heading: Runs of length 2<sup>k</sup> − 1
html: The runs between single 1s have lengths 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, 127, 255, ... in 99.6% of cases. Two runs of 2k − 1 with the 1 between them make 2k+1 − 1, so a merge of equal runs works like a carry in binary: s^127 1 s^127 becomes s^255. The groups separated by 1^3 0 look like the digits of a counter, with the far-left run (q^n r^m) feeding it. The left side, where the runs are swept, grows like the square root of the step count, and the right side like a smaller power (fitted exponent 0.31).

What halting would need. D reading a 1. D is reached only from C reading a 0, at a run boundary. A halt would need a boundary that the carries never seem to make. To decide it, one would prove the creation and merge of runs as rules on the run lengths, then show that the set of reachable run lists never contains the bad boundary.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.476). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.31).
After 109 steps the tape spans 45,385 cells (27,746 left of the start, 396 right), with a density of 1s of 0.683.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: The left side is the six-cell word 010111 repeated, cut into runs whose lengths are almost always 2^k − 1 and that merge in pairs (127 + 1 + 127 = 255), a binary-carry-like structure, swept by a bouncer.
family: bouncer with binary-carry runs of a periodic word
